families.title: Flat folds
families.mathematics: A paper disk creased along rays from its centre folds flat only if every crease turns the paper over, so neighbouring wedges face opposite ways: the number of creases is even, and the alternate wedges each add to a half-turn, 180° (Kawasaki; with free letters this is also enough). The letters must then pass more checks: three of one letter and one of the other on four creases, |M − V| = 2 in general (Maekawa); the two creases round a strictly smallest wedge differ (big-little-big); and folding away a smallest wedge leaves a smaller vertex that must fold too (crimp reduction, which decides every labelling). Four right angles fold in exactly the 8 labellings with an odd number of mountains, so tab stocks can fail by parity.
rules: Every ray is folded all the way flat, as a mountain (M) or a valley (V) seen from the yellow front.
Paper can’t pass through paper: layers may touch, but no fold may go through a layer.
Printed letters (dark) stay as they are.

puzzles.title: Flat folds playground
puzzles.objective: Crease a disk and fold it.
puzzles.instruction: Crease a disk and fold it.
puzzles.controls: A crease is a mountain (M) when it rises towards you from the yellow front and a valley (V) when it sinks away; the wedges are the pieces between the rays. Tap inside the disk away from the rays to add a ray, tap a ray or its letter to switch it between M and V, and press and hold a ray (or press Delete) to take it away. The round knob adds a ray too: drag it in, or use the arrow keys and Enter. Press Fold to fold it; Clear takes every ray away.
rules: Every ray is folded all the way flat, as a mountain (M) or a valley (V) seen from the yellow front.
Paper can’t pass through paper: layers may touch, but no fold may go through a layer.
Up to eight rays, on the ticks of the rim, 15° apart. Nothing needs finishing.
puzzles.idea: Free play with creases: add, label and remove rays and fold, to test guesses about which disks fold.
hints: Make four right angles and find every labelling that folds.
Try five rays. Can any letters fold it?
Move one ray of a folding disk by a tick. What happens at the seam?

parent.notice: Whether your child predicts the fold before pressing Fold, and which guesses they test.
parent.prompt: What do the disks that fold have in common?
parent.explanation: A single vertex folds flat exactly when it has an even number of creases, its alternate angles each add to 180° (Kawasaki), and the letters pass a check that the app makes by searching every order of the layers. Two more of one letter than of the other (Maekawa: |M − V| = 2) is necessary, and big-little-big and crimp reduction finish the job.
parent.extension: Make a disk with eight rays that folds, then change one letter so that it jams.
parent.connection: Single-vertex flat foldability: Kawasaki–Justin, Maekawa–Justin and Hull’s crimp reduction.

puzzles.provenance: Week 28 shared launch (crease a disk, label it from the marked front, and fold it) and Grades 2–3 Problem 3.

Drag the round knob round the rim, tap it, or tap near the rim, to put the new ray on a tick; arrow keys move the knob too. Tap a ray or its letter to switch it between M and V, then press Fold.

puzzles.idea: An even number of wedges whose every other wedge adds to a half-turn: the missing ray must make the wedge after ray 3 as big as the wedge after ray 2.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count ticks (15° each) and add two or three angles to 180°.
hints: Put the new ray somewhere, label every ray, and press Fold. Look at where the two ends of the strip land.
Folded flat, the wedges after rays 1 and 3 point one way and the other two point back. Each pair has to make a half-turn, 180°.
The wedge after ray 1 is 60°, so the wedge after ray 3 must be 120°: put the new ray 8 ticks after ray 3.

parent.notice: Whether your child places the ray by looking (opposite ray 2, a mirror image) or by counting ticks, and what the gap at the seam tells them after a fold.
parent.prompt: The ends missed. Which way should the new ray move?
parent.explanation: With rays at 0°, 60° and 180° the wedges are 60°, 120°, then two wedges that share the last 180°. Folding flat turns the paper over at every crease, so the wedges after rays 1 and 3 point one way and the other two back; the strip closes only when 60° and the wedge after ray 3 make 180°, so that wedge is 120° and the new ray is at 300°, the mirror image of ray 2. Then 6 of the 16 labellings fold: three of one letter and one of the other, with the new ray, ray 1 and ray 2 (round the two 60° wedges) not all the same.
parent.extension: Try rays at 0°, 30° and 180°, and at 0°, 120° and 180°.
parent.connection: Kawasaki’s theorem: one vertex folds flat exactly when its alternating angles each add to 180° (with free mountains and valleys).

puzzles.provenance: Week 28 Grades 2–3 Problem 4, pattern B (rays at 0°, 60° and 180°): “Add one ray to each pattern so the two alternating groups of wedges both make a half-turn. Make a flat fold of each completed pattern.”

puzzles.title: Two mountains printed
puzzles.objective: Label the open rays so that the disk folds flat, or show that it can’t.
puzzles.instruction: Label the open rays so that the disk folds flat, or show that it can’t.
puzzles.controls: A crease is a mountain (M) when it rises towards you from the yellow front and a valley (V) when it sinks away; the wedges are the pieces between the rays. Tap a ray or its letter to switch it between M and V, then press Fold to see the rim of the disk folded up from the side. If you think it can’t be done, press Can’t after a fold, tap each wedge to colour it yellow or green, and press Check.
rules: Every ray is folded all the way flat, as a mountain (M) or a valley (V) seen from the yellow front.
Paper can’t pass through paper: layers may touch, but no fold may go through a layer.
Printed letters (dark) stay as they are.
Can’t: after a fold, press Can’t, colour each wedge by the side it would show facing up, and press Check.
puzzles.idea: Three of one letter and one of the other, and the two small wedges side by side can’t be rolled up one way.
puzzles.prerequisites: No arithmetic needed to fold; reading the degrees on the wedges, and adding two or three of them, helps with the reason a disk can’t fold.
hints: Label rays 3 and 4 and press Fold. Watch the strip.
Four creases fold with three of one letter and one of the other, so rays 3 and 4 need one M and one V.
Make ray 3 a mountain and ray 4 a valley.

parent.notice: Whether your child tries MMMM or MMVV first, and what the jam looks like when rays 4, 1 and 2 are all mountains.
parent.prompt: Rays 3 and 4 need one of each. Which way round?
parent.explanation: Four creases fold with three of one letter and one of the other (Maekawa), so rays 3 and 4 are M and V in some order. The two 60° wedges sit side by side across ray 1, between the 120° wedges. If rays 4, 1 and 2 all bend the same way, the pair can’t tuck in between the 120° wedges: the fold along ray 1 ends up inside them, and they would have to pass through it (the app marks where). So ray 4 is the valley: MMMV, the only way.
parent.extension: With no printed letters, how many of the 16 labellings fold? (Six.)
parent.connection: Maekawa’s theorem (|M − V| = 2) and the generalized big-little-big lemma for a run of equal smallest angles.

puzzles.provenance: Week 28 Grades 4–5 Problem 1, pattern C (60°, 120°, 120°, 60°); the printed mountains on rays 1 and 2 are new, so that random letters fold one time in four.

Each tab is an M or a V for one open ray. Tap an open ray to put a tab on it (M, then V, then off), and press Fold when every tab is on. If you think it can’t be done, press Can’t after a fold, tap each disk until it shows the tabs that disk can take (one M and one V, or two the same), and press Check.

Each tab labels one open ray, and every tab is used. Can’t: after a fold, press Can’t, tap each disk until it shows the tabs it can take, and press Check.
puzzles.idea: Each right-angle disk folds with one or three mountains, so the printed letters decide how many M tabs each disk can take.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count to six and keep track of tabs used. No reading beyond M, V and the disk letters.
hints: Put the tabs on and press Fold. Which disks fold?
A disk of four right angles folds with three of one letter and one of the other. Disks B and C each need one M tab.
Disk A takes two V tabs. Disks B and C take one M and one V each.

parent.notice: Whether your child finishes one disk at a time, and what they do when the M tabs run out before disk C.
parent.prompt: Which disk can manage with no M tabs?
parent.explanation: A right-angle disk folds exactly when it has three of one letter and one of the other, that is one or three mountains. Disk A (M ? V ?) takes no M tab (MVVV) or two (MMVM); disks B (M M ? ?) and C (V ? V ?) take exactly one each. With two M tabs, disk A gets none, and B and C one each: 2 × 2 = 4 ways.
parent.extension: With four M tabs and two V tabs? (Also four ways, with disk A taking two.)
parent.connection: Maekawa’s theorem on four right angles: the 8 foldable labellings are the ones with an odd number of mountains.

puzzles.provenance: Week 28 K–1 Problem 4, row A: disks M?V?, MM?? and V?V? with 2 M and 4 V tabs, “use its six tabs to finish the disks.”

puzzles.idea: Every crease turns the paper over, so the wedges face up and down in turn; with an odd number of creases two neighbours face the same way.
puzzles.prerequisites: No arithmetic needed: counting the rays and following which way each wedge faces is enough.
hints: Label the open rays and press Fold. Look at the two ends of the strip.
Every crease turns the paper over. Which wedges face up when it is folded?
Going round, the wedges face up, down, up, down, up, down, up: the two wedges beside ray 1 both face up, though ray 1 is a crease.

parent.notice: Whether your child changes letters for a long time, or starts to wonder whether letters can fix it at all.
parent.prompt: If the wedge after ray 1 faces up, which way does the next one face? And the one before ray 1?
parent.explanation: Each crease turns the paper over, so neighbouring wedges face opposite ways when folded flat. Round seven wedges that goes up, down, up, down, up, down, up, and the last wedge meets the first at ray 1 facing the same way, though ray 1 is a crease. So seven creases can never fold flat, whatever the angles and letters. The certificate is a colouring with exactly one pair of matching neighbours: an odd ring can’t be coloured alternately. A random colouring passes 14 times in 128.
parent.extension: Does the same happen with three creases? With five?
parent.connection: A flat-foldable vertex has an even number of creases: the faces are properly 2-coloured by which side faces up.

puzzles.provenance: Week 28 Grades 4–5 Problem 2, pattern C (30°, 30°, 60°, 60°, 60°, 60°, 60°): “Can any of these patterns close flat along every ray?” The printed mountain on ray 1 and valley on ray 4 are new.

puzzles.idea: Around a wedge smaller than both its neighbours, the two creases must bend opposite ways (big-little-big).
puzzles.prerequisites: No arithmetic needed to fold; reading the degrees on the wedges, and adding two or three of them, helps with the reason a disk can’t fold.
hints: Label rays 1 and 4 and press Fold. Watch the slim wedge.
The 30° wedge is smaller than both neighbours, so rays 1 and 2 must bend opposite ways.
Make ray 1 a mountain and ray 4 a valley.

parent.notice: Whether your child counts letters (three of one, one of the other) and is surprised that VVVM still jams.
parent.prompt: Rays 1 and 2 both fold the slim wedge. What happens if they bend the same way?
parent.explanation: The counting rule leaves VVVM and MVVV. The 30° wedge lies between bigger wedges (120° and 60°). If rays 1 and 2 bend the same way, the slim wedge can’t tuck in: the fold along ray 2 ends up inside the bigger wedges, which would have to pass through it. So ray 1 is a mountain, opposite ray 2, and ray 4 is the valley: MVVV. Counting and angles together still do not settle a labelling.
parent.extension: With no printed letters, how many labellings fold? (Four: MVMM, MVVV, VMMM and VMVV.)
parent.connection: The big-little-big lemma: the creases round a strictly smallest angle have opposite letters.

puzzles.provenance: Week 28 Grades 4–5 Problem 1, pattern D (30°, 60°, 150°, 120°); the printed valleys on rays 2 and 3 are new, chosen so that letters that pass the counting rule (VVVM) still jam.

puzzles.idea: A parity certificate: the M tabs a set of disks can use come in fixed odd and even amounts, and the stock can miss them all.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count to six and keep track of tabs used. No reading beyond M, V and the disk letters.
hints: Put the tabs on and press Fold. Can you make every disk fold?
A right-angle disk folds with one or three mountains. How many M tabs can each disk take?
Disks B and C need one M tab each, and disk A takes none or two: 2 or 4 M tabs, never 3.

parent.notice: Whether your child keeps moving tabs, and when they start counting what each disk can take instead.
parent.prompt: How many M tabs can disk A take? And disk B?
parent.explanation: Each disk folds with one or three mountains. Disk A (M ? V ?) takes 0 or 2 M tabs, and disks B and C take exactly 1 each, so the three disks use 2 or 4 M tabs, never 3. The certificate marks each disk with the tabs it can take: disks B and C one M tab and one V tab, disk A two the same. In parity terms: three folded disks have an odd number of mountains, but the printed three plus three tabs make six.
parent.extension: Which stocks of six tabs work? (2 or 4 M tabs.)
parent.connection: A parity invariant from Maekawa’s theorem; the worksheet’s concrete proof sets the two choices for disk A beside the forced one-M disks.

puzzles.provenance: Week 28 K–1 Problem 4, row B: the same disks with 3 M and 3 V tabs, which can’t be done (guide p. 8, “Why row B cannot work”).

puzzles.title: Where does it go?
puzzles.objective: Add one ray so that the disk folds flat, and fold it.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Add a ray so the disk folds flat.
puzzles.instruction: Add one ray so that the disk folds flat, and fold it.
puzzles.controls: A crease is a mountain (M) when it rises towards you from the yellow front and a valley (V) when it sinks away; the wedges are the pieces between the rays. Drag the round knob round the rim, tap it, or tap near the rim, to put the new ray on a tick; arrow keys move the knob too. Tap a ray or its letter to switch it between M and V, then press Fold.

The new ray goes on a tick of the rim; the ticks are 15° apart.
puzzles.idea: The new ray is placed by the half-turn rule, not by symmetry: no ray here is a mirror of another.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count ticks (15° each) and add two or three angles to 180°.
hints: Put the new ray somewhere, label every ray, and press Fold. How far apart do the ends land?
The wedges after rays 1 and 3 must make 180° together, and so must the other two. The wedge after ray 1 is 60°.
The wedge after ray 3 must be 120°: put the new ray 8 ticks after ray 3.

parent.notice: Whether your child places the ray opposite one of the others (a guess from puzzle 1) and uses the gap to correct it.
parent.prompt: Which wedges point the same way when it is folded?
parent.explanation: The wedges are 60°, 90°, then two wedges sharing the last 210°. The wedges after rays 1 and 3 must add to 180°, so the wedge after ray 3 is 120° and the new ray is at 270° (the last wedge is then 90°, and 90 + 90 = 180 too). Then 4 of the 16 labellings fold: the counting rule, with the creases round the 60° wedge bending opposite ways.
parent.extension: Can you add a ray to rays at 0°, 60° and 150° so that it folds with a different ray? (No: the half-turn rule fixes the place.)
parent.connection: Kawasaki’s theorem fixes the last angle: with all but one ray placed, at most one position closes.

puzzles.provenance: New, in the form of Week 28 Grades 2–3 Problem 4 (add one ray so the alternating groups make half-turns), with rays at 0°, 60° and 150° so that the answer is not a mirror image.

puzzles.idea: Every other wedge must make a half-turn; when the alternate wedges add to 135° and 225°, no letters can close the disk.
puzzles.prerequisites: No arithmetic needed to fold; reading the degrees on the wedges, and adding two or three of them, helps with the reason a disk can’t fold.
hints: Label every ray and press Fold. Look at where the ends of the strip land.
Folded flat, every other wedge points the same way, and each set has to make a half-turn, 180°.
The wedges after rays 1 and 3 make 45 + 90 = 135°, and the other two make 90 + 135 = 225°.

parent.notice: Whether your child keeps relabelling, or notices that the gap at the seam is the same size whatever the letters.
parent.prompt: The gap is the same every time. What could change it?
parent.explanation: Folding flat turns the paper over at every crease, so the wedges lie alternately one way and back. Going round, the rim travels 45° forward, 90° back, 90° forward and 135° back: it ends 90° from where it started, whatever the letters, so the seam can’t close. The certificate is the two fans: the wedges after rays 1 and 3 make 135°, the other two 225°, and each would have to be a half-turn.
parent.extension: Move one ray so that it folds. (Move ray 4 three ticks on, from 225° to 270°: then 45 + 135 and 90 + 90 both make 180°.)
parent.connection: Kawasaki’s condition is necessary: the alternating sums must both be 180°.

puzzles.provenance: Week 28 Grades 4–5 Problem 1, pattern B (45°, 90°, 90°, 135°), and Problem 3, pattern A: “Explain why every other sector must total 180°.”

puzzles.idea: A run of equal slim wedges folds away like a zigzag and its creases split evenly; with big-little-big and the counting rule, that leaves 2 of the 32 labellings.
puzzles.prerequisites: No arithmetic needed to fold; reading the degrees on the wedges, and adding two or three of them, helps with the reason a disk can’t fold.
hints: Label the open rays and press Fold. Where does it jam?
Rays 1 to 4 border three 30° wedges in a row between bigger wedges: they need two of each letter. Rays 6 and 7, round the other 30° wedge, need one of each.
Eight creases fold with five of one letter and three of the other. Make rays 3, 4 and 8 mountains, and rays 6 and 7 one mountain and one valley.

parent.notice: Whether your child works on the run of slim wedges first, or changes letters one at a time and watches where the jam moves.
parent.prompt: Rays 1 and 2 are valleys. What must rays 3 and 4 be for the three slim wedges to fold away?
parent.explanation: Three 30° wedges in a row lie between 60° wedges. Folded flat they zigzag, and the four rays round them (rays 1 to 4) take two mountains and two valleys; rays 1 and 2 are printed valleys, so rays 3 and 4 are mountains. The other 30° wedge is smaller than both its neighbours, so rays 6 and 7 differ (big-little-big). Eight creases fold with five of one letter and three of the other (Maekawa): rays 3, 4 and 5 and one of rays 6 and 7 are mountains, so ray 8 is the fifth. Both VVMMMMVM and VVMMMVMM fold, and the app accepts either; the three rules leave only these 2 of the 32 labellings.
parent.extension: With no printed letters, how many of the 256 labellings fold? (24.)
parent.connection: The generalized big-little-big lemma (a run of equal smallest wedges), Maekawa’s theorem and Hull’s crimp reduction, which decides every single-vertex labelling.

puzzles.provenance: New: eight creases with runs of slim wedges, extending Week 28 Grades 4–5 Problem 3 (pattern D has eight rays) and Problem 6 (six creases from 30°, 60° and 90° wedges). The printed letters (valleys on rays 1 and 2, a mountain on ray 5) are chosen so that 2 of the 32 completions fold.

puzzles.prerequisites: No arithmetic needed to fold; reading the degrees on the wedges, and adding two or three of them, helps with the reason a disk can’t fold.

parent.notice: Whether your child uses the colouring from the four-ray disks, or starts again with letters.
parent.prompt: Which wedges point the same way when it is folded?
parent.explanation: Folded flat, the wedges alternate forward and back: 30 − 30 + 30 − 60 + 90 − 120 = −60, so the rim ends 60° short of closing whatever the letters, printed or chosen. The certificate is the two fans: the wedges after rays 1, 3 and 5 make 150° and the others 210°, not two half-turns.
parent.extension: Reorder the same six angles so that the disk folds with your own letters. (30°, 30°, 30°, 60°, 120°, 90° works: 30 + 30 + 120 and 30 + 60 + 90 both make 180°. Of the orders that start with 30°, 18 work.)

puzzles.provenance: Week 28 Grades 4–5 Problem 3, pattern C (30°, 30°, 30°, 60°, 90°, 120°). The printed valleys on rays 1, 3 and 5 are new: letters can’t close a gap.

puzzles.title: Four disks
puzzles.objective: Use every tab so that every disk folds flat, or show that it can’t be done.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Use every tab so all the disks fold.
puzzles.instruction: Use every tab so that every disk folds flat, or show that it can’t be done.
puzzles.controls: A crease is a mountain (M) when it rises towards you from the yellow front and a valley (V) when it sinks away; the wedges are the pieces between the rays. Each tab is an M or a V for one open ray. Tap an open ray to put a tab on it (M, then V, then off), and press Fold when every tab is on. If you think it can’t be done, press Can’t after a fold, tap each disk until it shows the tabs that disk can take (one M and one V, or two the same), and press Check.
rules: Every ray is folded all the way flat, as a mountain (M) or a valley (V) seen from the yellow front.
Paper can’t pass through paper: layers may touch, but no fold may go through a layer.
Printed letters (dark) stay as they are.
Each tab labels one open ray, and every tab is used. Can’t: after a fold, press Can’t, tap each disk until it shows the tabs it can take, and press Check.
puzzles.idea: Disks that need exactly one M tab are settled first; the disks that take none or two then share what is left.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count to six and keep track of tabs used. No reading beyond M, V and the disk letters.
hints: Put the tabs on and press Fold. Which disks fold?
Disks A and B need one M tab each. Disks C and D each take none or two.
One of disks C and D takes two M tabs and the other takes two V tabs.

parent.notice: Whether your child sorts the disks by what they can take before placing tabs, or places tabs and repairs.
parent.prompt: How many M tabs are left once disks A and B have theirs?
parent.explanation: Every right-angle disk folds with one or three mountains. Disks A (M M ? ?) and B (V ? V ?) take exactly one M tab each. Disks C (M ? V ?) and D (? M ? V) take none or two. With four M tabs, one of C and D takes two and the other none: 2 choices, times 2 ways for each of A and B, gives 8 ways.
parent.extension: Which stocks of eight tabs work? (2, 4 or 6 M tabs.)
parent.connection: The same parity bookkeeping as puzzle 6, with a real choice between disks.

puzzles.provenance: New: Week 28 K–1 Problem 4 extended to four disks and eight tabs.

puzzles.title: The last crease
puzzles.objective: Add one ray so that the disk folds flat, and fold it.
puzzles.visibleObjective: Add a ray so the disk folds flat.
puzzles.instruction: Add one ray so that the disk folds flat, and fold it.
puzzles.controls: A crease is a mountain (M) when it rises towards you from the yellow front and a valley (V) when it sinks away; the wedges are the pieces between the rays. Drag the round knob round the rim, tap it, or tap near the rim, to put the new ray on a tick; arrow keys move the knob too. Tap a ray or its letter to switch it between M and V, then press Fold.
rules: Every ray is folded all the way flat, as a mountain (M) or a valley (V) seen from the yellow front.
Paper can’t pass through paper: layers may touch, but no fold may go through a layer.
Printed letters (dark) stay as they are.
The new ray goes on a tick of the rim; the ticks are 15° apart.
puzzles.idea: With five rays given, the sixth is placed by the half-turn rule for three alternate wedges.
puzzles.prerequisites: Count ticks (15° each) and add two or three angles to 180°.
hints: Put the new ray somewhere, label every ray, and press Fold. How far apart do the ends land?
The wedges after rays 1, 3 and 5 must make 180° together. The first two are 30° and 60°.
The wedge after ray 5 must be 90°: put the new ray 6 ticks after ray 5.

parent.notice: Whether your child adds up alternate wedges before placing the ray, or moves it and watches the gap shrink.
parent.prompt: How big must the wedge after ray 5 be?
parent.explanation: The wedges are 30°, 60°, 60°, 90°, then two wedges sharing the last 120°. The wedges after rays 1, 3 and 5 must make 180°, so the wedge after ray 5 is 90° and the new ray is at 330° (the last wedge is 30°, and 60 + 90 + 30 = 180 too). Then 18 of the 64 labellings fold.
parent.extension: Move ray 5 to 210°. Where does the new ray go now? (At 300°.)
parent.connection: Kawasaki’s theorem for six creases fixes the last angle.

puzzles.provenance: New, in the form of Week 28 Grades 2–3 Problem 4, with six creases as in Grades 4–5 Problem 6.
